rationale: The book's core accounts for every listed occurrence by letting immediate context name the deeds while isolating the uniform economic claim Paul rejects (purchase of justification/Spirit/standing/debt). This fits the supplied texts more tightly than any fixed-class alternative: Rom 3:20/28 and Gal 3:10 explicitly invoke God's law and the Deuteronomic curse, Gal 2:16 arises inside the circumcision-party table-fellowship crisis, and Gal 3:2/5 leave the acts unnamed yet still deny them as the source of the Spirit. The traditional fixed-class reading (or its New-Perspective boundary-marker narrowing) must either ignore the contextual variation or expand 'boundary markers' until the label loses precision. The book's distinction between the deed itself and the rejected claim also coheres with the surrounding argument that faith establishes rather than voids the law (Rom 3:31) and that perfect obedience still creates no surplus wage (Luke 17:10; Rom 4:4). No material text is left unexplained, so the book is the better-supported identification.
book_core_identification: Paul's phrase for deeds considered in relation to law; the surrounding context identifies the particular deeds (God's law, a circumcision-party application, or unnamed acts), while the phrase itself consistently denies those deeds any power to purchase justification, produce the Spirit, establish covenant standing, or place God in debt.
book_secondary_elaborations: The phrase is not a synonym for obedience
It does not identify one unchanging class of deeds
Works are excluded only as purchase price / source of the gift and are restored as the life the gift produces
Paul's named modifiers (law of God, law of sin, law of Christ, etc.) control the referent of 'law' and prevent collapsing every occurrence into a single bucket
The economic contrast of wages/debt versus grace (Rom 4) and the telos reading of 'end of the law' supply the larger framework
strongest_counter_interpretation: The traditional Reformation/Protestant reading (still dominant at the popular level and still primary in the supplied common-interpretation summaries): 'works of the law' is a fixed technical phrase for any human deeds of obedience to the Mosaic Torah offered as the basis or means of justification, functioning as the negative pole in the faith-versus-works antithesis and symbolizing legalism or self-reliant merit.
counter_core_identification: A single, unchanging class of Mosaic-law deeds performed to earn or establish righteousness before God, uniformly opposed to justification by faith alone.
material_core_denial: The counter insists on one fixed class of deeds and therefore denies the book's claim that the referent is context-determined and that the phrase's consistent content is only the rejected purchase-price claim.
counter_case: Rom 3:20, 28 and Gal 2:16 repeatedly place 'works of the law' in direct antithesis to justification by faith
Gal 3:10 places those who are 'of the works of the law' under the Deuteronomic curse, suggesting the whole Mosaic code
The phrase is treated as Paul's technical shorthand for the entire faith-versus-works contrast, extended by parallel 'not of works' texts (Eph 2:8-9; Titus 3:5)
Popular and confessional usage has long equated the phrase with legalism or self-reliant achievement
book_explanatory_advantages: Explains why the same phrase can sit inside both an explicit citation of 'the book of the law' (Gal 3:10) and a circumcision-party table-fellowship dispute (Gal 2:12-16) without contradiction
Preserves Paul's positive statements about the law (Rom 3:31; 7:12, 22; 8:4) and about good works that follow the gift (Eph 2:10; Titus 3:8)
Accounts for the textual variant at Rom 9:32 (TR 'works of the law' versus critical 'as if by works') by focusing on the attempted manner rather than a code of deeds
Unifies the economic language of debt versus grace across Romans 4 and the 'works of the law' texts without equating obedience itself with the forbidden claim
counter_explanatory_advantages: Offers a simple, memorable slogan that maps cleanly onto the surface contrast of faith versus works in the most-cited verses
Aligns with centuries of confessional and catechetical usage
decisive_sources: The full proving chapter's classification table of every occurrence and its contextual controls
unresolved_objections: Some readers may still prefer a narrower New-Perspective restriction to boundary markers alone, even though that restriction fails for the explicit 'book of the law' citations
The precise relationship between the rejected purchase-price claim and later Spirit-enabled obedience remains a matter of systematic theology beyond the lexical scope of the entry
